title: When you land
body:
Carrasco International Airport (MVD) sits about 20 km east of downtown Montevideo. The official airport taxi desk (Taxis Aeropuerto Carrasco) runs a fixed-fare structure with its own calculator, and the trip takes roughly 25–30 minutes outside rush hour. ⚠ Public buses also run from the terminal to Tres Cruces and downtown for far less (≈45–60 minutes with luggage) — several lines are reported to cover the route, but confirm the current number at the terminal rather than relying on a specific line number here.

There is no direct flight from New York; every routing from JFK connects (commonly through São Paulo, Panama City, or Bogotá), so budget the full connection time on arrival day rather than a tight single hop.
checklist: Buy an Antel prepaid SIM chip at the airport arrivals area, or activate an eSIM before you fly
Have small USD or freshly-withdrawn UYU for the airport taxi if skipping the bus
Confirm your connecting-flight buffer at booking — no JFK–MVD route is nonstop

title: Local essentials
body:
Currency is the Uruguayan peso (UYU, "$" locally — watch for confusion with USD prices quoted the same way in tourist areas). Spanish is the national language, spoken in the fast, Italian-inflected Rioplatense accent shared with Buenos Aires ("vos" instead of "tú", "sh" for "ll/y"). Electrical outlets are mostly Type L (Italian 3-pin) and Type C, at 220V — a US traveler needs a plug adapter and, for 120V-only devices, a voltage converter.

Uruguay abolished daylight saving time in 2015, so it stays on UTC-3 year-round — no seasonal clock change to plan around.
checklist: Pack a Type L/C plug adapter — US flat-pin plugs do not fit
Check any 120V-only device for a 220V-compatible charger/converter

title: Entry & documents
body:
A US passport holder needs no visa for a tourist visit of up to 90 days — see the Entry card below. Immigration can ask for proof of onward travel and sufficient funds, though this is rarely enforced in practice for US arrivals.

⚠ The US State Department's current advisory level for Uruguay could not be automatically verified in this research pass (the page blocks plain automated fetches) — confirm the level at travel.state.gov before you go. A search lead (via the US Embassy Montevideo's own site) points to a Level 2 (Exercise Increased Caution) renewal around July 2026, but this is a lead, not a fetched primary verification.

title: Phone & data
body: Antel is the state carrier and the broadest network. A prepaid "Chip Prepago" SIM costs {{fact:antel-chip-65-uyu}} (plus a minimum top-up to activate service) from Antel's own stores; airport kiosks in the international arrivals area sell tourist-ready SIMs from Antel and Movistar, passport in hand for registration. Antel does not currently issue eSIMs to tourists arriving without a local contract — a third-party travel eSIM is the alternative if you want to skip the physical-SIM counter.

title: Booking checklist
checklist: Flights (no nonstop JFK–MVD — check your connection buffer)
Accommodation — confirm AC is real and working, not just listed
Airport transfer or Antel/eSIM data plan sorted before landing
Isla de Lobos boat excursion, if the weather looks settled (isladelobos.com.uy)

title: Public holidays
note: Checked automatically against your travel dates (source: Nager.Date, refreshed each deploy). Carnival Monday and Tuesday (Feb 8–9, 2027) fall inside this trip — they're normal business days by law (employers choose whether to grant them), but many offices, and some museums, run reduced hours or close. The Desfile de Llamadas parade itself is a separate, locally-scheduled event — see the Days tab.
